parts.prompt: The prism is melted down and recast into identical solid spheres, each of radius $15\,mm$.\nCalculate the maximum number of complete spheres that can be made, and find the volume of metal remaining, in cubic centimetres, correct to $1$ decimal place.

parts.prompt: A reviewer claims: "The box-and-whisker plots show that the mean battery life of Brand B is greater than $27$ hours, and that more batteries were tested for Brand B than for Brand A."\\[0.15cm]Give two reasons why the reviewer's claim is not valid from the given diagram.

Box-and-whisker plots do not show the sample size (number of batteries tested) for either brand [B1]

parts.label: (d)
parts.prompt: In a sample of $60$ Brand B batteries, estimate how many batteries lasted more than $21$ hours.
markscheme: $21$ hours is the lower quartile, so $\dfrac{3}{4} \times 60$ [M1]

intro_text: Two machines, Machine $A$ and Machine $B$, fill packets of coffee. A random sample of $40$ packets from each machine is weighed. The table shows summary statistics for the masses, in grams, of the packets in each sample.

parts.label: (a)
parts.prompt: Calculate the total mass of the $40$ packets in the sample from Machine $A$.

parts.label: (b)
parts.prompt: Make two statistical comparisons between the masses of the packets filled by Machine $A$ and Machine $B$.
markscheme: Average comparison: On average, Machine $B$ fills heavier packets because its median is higher ($251.0\text{ g} > 250.2\text{ g}$) (or Machine $A$ has a higher mean mass, $250.4\text{ g} > 249.8\text{ g}$) [B2] (or valid statement without quoting values [B1])

Spread comparison: Machine $A$ fills packets with more consistent masses because its interquartile range ($1.8\text{ g} < 3.4\text{ g}$) and range ($5.6\text{ g} < 11.2\text{ g}$) are smaller [B2] (or valid statement without quoting values [B1])

parts.label: (c)
parts.prompt: Explain why the median and interquartile range are more appropriate measures than the mean and range for comparing these two samples.
markscheme: Machine $B$ has a very large range ($11.2\text{ g}$) relative to its IQR ($3.4\text{ g}$) and its mean is lower than its median, indicating extreme low values (outliers) [B1]
The median and interquartile range are not distorted by extreme values / outliers [B1]

parts.label: (d)
parts.prompt: A supervisor claims that Machine $B$ must have produced at least one packet weighing less than $242$ g. Explain whether the supervisor's claim must be true.
markscheme: No, the claim does not have to be true because the minimum and maximum values are unknown [B1]
For example, the masses in Machine $B$ could range from $243.0$ g to $254.2$ g (giving a range of $11.2$ g and median $251.0$ g) with no packet below $242$ g [B1]

intro_text: The back-to-back stem-and-leaf diagram shows the test scores, out of $60$, of $15$ students in Class A and $15$ students in Class B.

parts.label: (a)
parts.prompt: For Class A, find:

subparts.label: (i)
subparts.prompt: the median score

subparts.label: (ii)
subparts.prompt: the interquartile range.

parts.label: (b)
parts.prompt: For Class B, the median score is $44$ and the interquartile range is $13$. Write down two comparisons between the test scores of Class A and Class B, supported by statistical values.
markscheme: On average, Class B scored higher than Class A because the median for Class B ($44$) is greater than the median for Class A ($38$) [B1]
The scores in Class B are more consistent (less spread out) than in Class A because the interquartile range for Class B ($13$) is smaller than for Class A ($16$) [B1]

parts.label: (c)
parts.prompt: One student from Class A and one student from Class B are chosen at random. Explain why the student from Class A could still have a higher score than the student from Class B, giving a specific example from the diagram.
markscheme: The distributions of scores overlap, so some individual scores in Class A are higher than some scores in Class B [B1]
For example, the highest score in Class A is $54$, which is higher than the lowest score in Class B of $28$ [B1]

parts.label: (d)
parts.prompt: Another class, Class C, has $30$ students and a mean test score of $41$. Calculate the combined mean test score of all $60$ students in Class A, Class B, and Class C.
markscheme: Total score for Class A $= 580$ and total score for Class B $= 650$ [M1]

intro_text: A research institute investigates the daily screen time, in minutes, of two groups of users: Group P (teenagers) and Group Q (adults). The table shows summary statistics for the two groups.

parts.label: (a)
parts.prompt: When Group P and Group Q are combined into a single group of $(80 + n)$ users, the overall mean daily screen time is $185$ minutes.\\[0.15cm]Calculate the value of $n$.

parts.label: (b)
parts.prompt: Compare the daily screen time of Group P and Group Q using the median and the interquartile range.
markscheme: Group P has a higher median screen time ($210$ minutes) than Group Q ($160$ minutes), so on average Group P spends more time on screens [B1]
Group P has a smaller interquartile range ($70$ minutes) than Group Q ($80$ minutes), so Group P's screen times are less spread out / more consistent [B1]

parts.label: (c)
parts.prompt: A journalist reads the table and concludes: "Because the mean daily screen time for Group P is $215$ minutes and for Group Q is $165$ minutes, every teenager in Group P spent more time on screens than the average adult in Group Q."\\[0.15cm]Explain why this conclusion is incorrect, and state one limitation of using only this table to compare all teenagers and adults.
markscheme: The mean is only an average; Group P's lower quartile is $175$ minutes, so at least $25\%$ of Group P users spent $175$ minutes or less (and some could spend less than $165$ minutes) [B1]
The table does not show extreme values (minimum/maximum) or how the samples were chosen, so results may not represent the wider populations [B1]

parts.label: (d)
parts.prompt: In a follow-up survey, $40$ additional adults are added to Group Q. Every one of these $40$ adults has a daily screen time of $100$ minutes.\\[0.15cm]State the new value of the lower quartile of Group Q, explaining your answer.
markscheme: Group Q now has $120 + 40 = 160$ users, so the lower quartile is at the $40$th ordered value ($25\%$ of $160 = 40$) [M1]
Since all $40$ new adults have a screen time of $100$ minutes (which is less than the previous lower quartile of $125$ minutes), at least the lowest $40$ values are now $100$ minutes [A1]

intro_text: The two pie charts show the distribution of customer complaints received by Store P and Store Q across four categories: Delivery, Quality, Pricing, and Service.

parts.label: (a)
parts.prompt: Find the value of $x$ in the pie chart for Store P.

parts.label: (b)
parts.prompt: A manager looks at the two pie charts and claims that Store P received more complaints about Delivery than Store Q because the sector angle for Delivery is larger in Store P ($126^\circ > 108^\circ$). Explain why the manager's claim may be incorrect.
markscheme: Pie charts only show proportions (or percentages) and not the total number of complaints at each store [B1]
If Store Q received a larger total number of complaints than Store P, Store Q could have more Delivery complaints [B1]

parts.label: (c)
parts.prompt: Store P received $140$ complaints about Delivery. Calculate the total number of complaints received by Store P.

parts.label: (d)
parts.prompt: Store Q received $80$ more complaints in total than Store P. Calculate how many more complaints Store Q received about Quality than Store P.
markscheme: Total complaints for Store Q $= 400 + 80 = 480$, so Quality for Store Q $= \dfrac{135}{360} \times 480 = 180$ [M1]

parts.label: (e)
parts.prompt: In the following month, Store P reduces its Delivery complaints by $20\%$ and its Pricing complaints by $15\%$, while the number of Quality and Service complaints remains unchanged. Calculate the new sector angle for Delivery when a new pie chart is drawn for Store P.
markscheme: Original Pricing complaints $= \dfrac{72}{360} \times 400 = 80$, so new Pricing complaints $= 80 \times 0.85 = 68$ [M1]

intro_text: The cumulative frequency diagram shows information about the journey times, $t$ minutes, of $80$ Train commuters and $80$ Bus commuters.

parts.label: (a)
parts.prompt: Use the cumulative frequency diagram to find

subparts.label: (i)
subparts.prompt: the median journey time for Train commuters,

subparts.label: (ii)
subparts.prompt: the interquartile range of the journey times for Bus commuters.

parts.label: (b)
parts.prompt: One of the $80$ Bus commuters is selected at random. Estimate the probability that this commuter's journey time is more than $44$ minutes.

parts.label: (c)
parts.prompt: Compare the journey times of Train commuters and Bus commuters, referring to both an average and a measure of spread.
markscheme: Bus median $= 38$ minutes and Train IQR $= 36 - 20 = 16$ minutes [B1]
Train commuters have shorter journey times on average because the median is lower ($30\text{ min} < 38\text{ min}$) [B1]
Train journey times are more consistent because the interquartile range is smaller ($16\text{ min} < 24\text{ min}$) [B1]

parts.label: (d)
parts.prompt: A local newspaper publishes this diagram with the headline: "More people commute by Bus than by Train in this city." Give two distinct reasons why this conclusion cannot be validly drawn from the given data.
markscheme: Equal fixed sample sizes ($80$ commuters each) were surveyed, so the total number of Train or Bus commuters in the city is unknown [B1]
The diagram only measures journey times (and the samples may not be representative of the whole city) [B1]

parts.label: (e)
parts.prompt: In a separate survey of $120$ Car commuters, $35\%$ of the commuters had a journey time of $30$ minutes or less. Explain why it is not possible to determine the exact number of commuters in this survey whose journey time was strictly less than $30$ minutes.
markscheme: $35\%$ of $120 = 42$ commuters took $30$ minutes or less ($t \le 30$), which includes commuters who took exactly $30$ minutes [B1]
The exact number of commuters whose journey time was equal to $30$ minutes is unknown [B1]

intro_text: A survey of $20$ households in a village records four variables for each household.

parts.label: (a)
parts.prompt: Complete the table below by writing either Discrete or Continuous for each variable.
markscheme: Discrete, Continuous, Discrete, Continuous in order [B2]
Award [B1] if two or three classifications are correct

parts.label: (b)
parts.prompt: Explain why the floor area of a house is continuous data whereas the number of bedrooms is discrete data.
markscheme: Floor area is measured and can take any value within a range, so it is continuous [B1]
Number of bedrooms is counted and can only take exact whole number values, so it is discrete [B1]

parts.label: (c)
parts.prompt: The numbers of vehicles owned by the $20$ households are listed below. \[0.15cm] \begin{center} $1$ \quad $0$ \quad $2$ \quad $1$ \quad $3$ \quad $2$ \quad $1$ \\[0.15cm] $0$ \quad $2$ \quad $1$ \quad $4$ \quad $2$ \quad $1$ \quad $0$ \\[0.15cm] $2$ \quad $3$ \quad $2$ \quad $2$ \quad $1$ \quad $2$ \end{center}

subparts.label: (i)
subparts.prompt: Write down the modal number of vehicles owned.

subparts.label: (ii)
subparts.prompt: Find the median number of vehicles owned.

intro_text: A school nurse conducts a health and fitness survey of students and records four variables.

parts.label: (a)
parts.prompt: Complete the table by writing Discrete or Continuous for each variable.
markscheme: All four rows completed correctly: Discrete, Continuous, Discrete, Continuous [B2]
If [B2] is not awarded, award [B1] for two or three rows completed correctly

parts.label: (b)
parts.prompt: Explain why the height of a student is continuous data whereas shoe size is discrete data.
markscheme: Height is measured and can take any value within a given range [B1]
Shoe size can only take specific fixed values (integers or half-sizes) with no intermediate values [B1]

parts.label: (c)
parts.context: The nurse groups the heights, $h$ cm, of $40$ students into class intervals: $140 \le h < 150$, $150 \le h < 160$, $160 \le h < 170$ and $170 \le h < 180$.

subparts.label: (i)
subparts.prompt: Explain why inequality signs ($\le$ and $<$) are used to define these intervals instead of writing $140 - 149$ and $150 - 159$.
markscheme: Height is continuous data, so a student could have a height between $149$ cm and $150$ cm (such as $149.5$ cm) which would otherwise fall into a gap [B1]

subparts.label: (ii)
subparts.prompt: A student has a height of exactly $160$ cm.\nWrite down the class interval in which this student is recorded.

intro_text: A sports scientist collects four sets of numerical data from a group of $24$ athletes during a training session.

parts.label: (a)
parts.prompt: Complete the table by writing whether each type of data is discrete or continuous.
markscheme: Discrete, Continuous, Continuous, Discrete [B2] (or three correct [B1])

parts.label: (b)
parts.prompt: Explain the difference between discrete data and continuous data.
markscheme: Discrete data can only take specific exact values (usually whole numbers obtained by counting) [B1]
Continuous data can take any value within a given range (obtained by measuring) [B1]

parts.label: (c)
parts.prompt: The sports scientist also records the number of energy bars eaten by each of the $24$ athletes. The results are shown below. \[0.15cm] \begin{center} $0$ \quad $1$ \quad $2$ \quad $1$ \quad $3$ \quad $0$ \quad $2$ \quad $1$ \\[0.15cm] $4$ \quad $2$ \quad $1$ \quad $0$ \quad $2$ \quad $3$ \quad $1$ \quad $2$ \\[0.15cm] $1$ \quad $0$ \quad $2$ \quad $1$ \quad $3$ \quad $2$ \quad $1$ \quad $1$ \end{center} Calculate the mean number of energy bars eaten per athlete.

intro_text: Do not use a calculator in this question.\\[0.15cm]During a school sports day, four pieces of data are recorded for each competitor.

parts.label: (a)
parts.prompt: Complete the table by placing a tick ($\checkmark$) in the correct column for each variable. The first row has been completed for you.
markscheme: Time taken to run $100$ m ticked as Continuous [B1]
Height of high jump cleared ticked as Continuous [B1]

parts.label: (b)
parts.prompt: Explain why the height of the high jump cleared is continuous data, even though the results are recorded to the nearest centimetre.
markscheme: Height is measured and can take any value within a continuous range [B1]
Recording to the nearest centimetre only rounds the measurement and does not make the variable discrete [B1]

parts.label: (c)
parts.prompt: In the long jump event, a competitor's jump is recorded as $4.65$ m, correct to the nearest centimetre.\\[0.15cm]Write down the lower bound and the upper bound of the actual length of the jump.
parts.answer_format: Lower bound = ..... m , Upper bound = ..... m

intro_text:
An environmental scientist monitors weather conditions in a coastal town over $40$ days.
Each day, the scientist records the daily rainfall, $r$ mm, measured to the nearest $0.1$ mm.
A day is classified as a dry day if $r = 0$, and a rainy day if $r > 0$.
The table shows the distribution of daily rainfall for the $40$ days.

parts.label: (a)
parts.prompt: Explain why the number of rainy days is discrete data whereas the daily rainfall $r$ is continuous data.
markscheme: The number of rainy days is obtained by counting and can only take whole-number values [B1]
Daily rainfall is obtained by measuring and can take any value on a continuous scale [B1]

parts.label: (b)
parts.prompt: Using mid-interval values for the continuous intervals, the estimated mean daily rainfall for all $40$ days is $11.5$ mm.\nForm two equations in $x$ and $y$ and solve them to find the value of $x$ and the value of $y$.

parts.label: (c)
parts.prompt: Because the daily rainfall is recorded to the nearest $0.1$ mm, a reading of $20.0$ mm is placed in the interval $10 < r \le 20$, while a reading of $20.1$ mm is the smallest reading placed in the interval $20 < r \le 40$.\nWrite down the lower bound of the actual rainfall for a reading of $20.1$ mm.

parts.label: (d)
parts.prompt: One of the $40$ days is chosen at random.\nGiven that it was a rainy day, calculate the probability that the recorded rainfall was more than $10$ mm, giving your answer as a fraction in its simplest form.

intro_text: Do not use a calculator in this question.\\[0.15cm]A botanist investigates $100$ plants in a greenhouse. The stem length, $L$ cm, of each plant is continuous data, recorded to the nearest centimetre in the table.

subparts.label: (i)
subparts.prompt: Explain why there appears to be a gap between $14$ cm and $15$ cm in the table even though stem length is continuous data.
markscheme: The lengths were rounded to the nearest centimetre, so values between $14.5$ cm and $15$ cm are rounded up into $15 - 19$ and values below $14.5$ cm are rounded down into $10 - 14$ [B1]

subparts.label: (ii)
subparts.prompt: Write down the true continuous class interval for the group recorded as $15 - 19$ cm, giving your answer in the form $a \le L < b$.

parts.label: (b)
parts.prompt: A histogram is drawn to represent the continuous stem length distribution.\\[0.15cm]On the histogram, the bar representing the recorded group $15 - 19$ cm has width $2$ cm and height $10$ cm.

subparts.label: (i)
subparts.prompt: Calculate the width and the height of the bar representing the recorded group $20 - 29$ cm.
markscheme: True class width $= 29.5 - 19.5 = 10$ cm (twice $5$ cm), so bar width $= 4$ cm [B1]
Frequency density $= \dfrac{40}{10} = 4$ (compared to $\dfrac{25}{5} = 5$), so bar height $= \dfrac{4}{5} \times 10 = 8$ cm [B1]

subparts.label: (ii)
subparts.prompt: Calculate the height of the bar representing the recorded group $30 - 44$ cm, giving your answer as a fraction in its simplest form.
markscheme: True class width $= 44.5 - 29.5 = 15$ cm, so frequency density $= \dfrac{20}{15} = \dfrac{4}{3}$ [M1]

parts.label: (c)
parts.prompt: For the same $100$ plants, the number of leaves on each plant is discrete data.\\[0.15cm]- $k$ plants have $4$ leaves.\\[0.15cm]- $(2k + 3)$ plants have $5$ leaves.\\[0.15cm]- $(3k - 1)$ plants have $6$ leaves.\\[0.15cm]- $2k$ plants have $7$ leaves.\\[0.15cm]- $18$ plants have $8$ leaves.

subparts.label: (i)
subparts.prompt: Show that $k = 10$.

subparts.label: (ii)
subparts.prompt: Find the median number of leaves and calculate the exact mean number of leaves per plant.
markscheme: Frequencies are $10, 23, 29, 20, 18$; $50$th and $51$st values give Median $= 6$ [B1]

intro_text: A quality-control engineer inspects batches of precision steel rods. Two variables are recorded: $d$, the number of defective rods in a batch, and $L$, the length of a rod in millimetres. In a sample of $40$ batches, the distribution of $d$ is shown in the table below, where $x$ and $y$ are positive integers. The mean number of defective rods per batch is $1.25$.

parts.label: (a)
parts.prompt: Form two simultaneous equations in $x$ and $y$, and solve them to find the value of $x$ and the value of $y$.

parts.label: (b)
parts.prompt: Find the median and the interquartile range of $d$, the number of defective rods per batch.

parts.label: (c)
parts.prompt: A trainee records the lengths, $L$ mm, of a sample of rods using the intervals $50$ to $54$, $55$ to $59$, and $60$ to $64$. Explain why this notation is suitable for discrete data such as $d$, but unsuitable for continuous data such as $L$.
markscheme: For discrete data, values only take integers so no values exist between $54$ and $55$ [B1]
For continuous data, measurements can take decimal values between $54$ and $55$ (such as $54.3$ mm), leaving gaps unless written as continuous inequalities [B1]

parts.label: (d)
parts.prompt: The lengths, $L$ mm, of $60$ rods are correctly grouped into continuous intervals: $18$ rods have $49.5 \le L < 54.5$, $30$ rods have $54.5 \le L < 59.5$, and $12$ rods have $59.5 \le L < 64.5$. Calculate the greatest possible value of the mean length of the $60$ rods.

intro_text: A quality-control engineer inspects a random sample of $50$ machined metal bolts.\nThe table shows the number of surface defects ($d$) found on each bolt.

subparts.label: (i)
subparts.prompt: Calculate the mean number of surface defects per bolt.

subparts.label: (ii)
subparts.prompt: Explain why the mean number of surface defects can be a non-integer value for other samples even though $d$ is discrete data.
markscheme: The mean is a calculated numerical average across all bolts in the sample rather than a count of defects on a single bolt [B1]

parts.label: (b)
parts.context: The masses, $m$ grams, of the same $50$ bolts are measured as continuous data and grouped into the frequency table below.

subparts.label: (i)
subparts.prompt: Calculate an estimate of the mean mass of a bolt.

subparts.label: (ii)
subparts.prompt: A bolt is rejected if its mass is $51.0$ g or more, or if it has more than $2$ surface defects.\nState the maximum possible number of bolts that could be rejected from this sample of $50$ bolts, explaining your reasoning.
markscheme: There are $9$ bolts with $m \ge 51.0$ g and $4 + 2 = 6$ bolts with $d > 2$; the maximum total occurs if none of these bolts overlap ($9 + 6 = 15$) [B1]

intro_text: A courier company records two variables for each of $60$ deliveries made in one week:\\[0.15cm]- the number of parcels, $n$, in each delivery (Table 1),\\[0.15cm]- the total mass, $m$ kg, of each delivery (Table 2).

parts.label: (a)
parts.prompt: Explain why continuous inequality intervals such as $0 < m \le 5$ are used in Table 2, whereas single integers are used in Table 1.
markscheme: Mass is continuous data and can take any decimal value between boundaries, so inequality intervals prevent gaps or overlaps [B1]
Number of parcels is discrete data and can only take exact whole-number values [B1]

parts.label: (b)
parts.prompt: Calculate the mean number of parcels per delivery, giving your answer as a fraction in its simplest form.

parts.label: (c)
parts.prompt: Calculate an estimate of the mean mass of a delivery.

parts.label: (d)
parts.prompt: Explain why the mean calculated in part (c) is only an estimate, whereas the mean calculated in part (b) is exact.
markscheme: In Table 2 the continuous data is grouped so individual masses are unknown and mid-interval values are used as approximations, whereas in Table 1 every exact discrete value is known [B1]

intro_text: A marine biologist studies a sample of $50$ adult sea turtles. For each turtle, the biologist records $n$, the number of barnacles attached to its shell, and $m$, the mass of the turtle in kilograms, measured to the nearest $0.1$ kg. The masses of the $50$ turtles are summarised in the table below.

parts.label: (a)
parts.prompt: State which variable, $n$ or $m$, is discrete data and which variable is continuous data, giving a reason for each choice.
markscheme: $n$ is discrete because the number of barnacles is counted and can only take whole number values [B1]
$m$ is continuous because mass is measured and can take any value within a continuous range [B1]

parts.label: (b)
parts.prompt: Use the table of masses to answer the following.

subparts.label: (i)
subparts.prompt: Explain why the masses are grouped into class intervals using inequalities such as $30.0 \le m < 35.0$ rather than listing individual values.
markscheme: Continuous measurements can take any decimal value in a range (so individual values rarely repeat) and inequalities group all possible values without gaps or overlaps [B1]

subparts.label: (ii)
subparts.prompt: Calculate an estimate of the mean mass of the $50$ turtles.
markscheme: Mid-interval values $32.5$, $37.5$, $42.5$, and $47.5$ seen or used [M1]

parts.label: (c)
parts.prompt: Because each mass $m$ was measured to the nearest $0.1$ kg, a turtle recorded as having a mass of $35.0$ kg actually has a true mass $w$ kg in the interval $a \le w < b$. Write down the values of $a$ and $b$.

parts.label: (d)
parts.prompt: The discrete variable $n$ has a mean of $14.6$ barnacles for the $50$ turtles. Explain why the mean of a discrete variable can be a decimal number even though the data values themselves can only be integers.
markscheme: The mean is calculated by dividing the total number of barnacles ($730$) by $50$, which does not have to result in a whole number [B1]

intro_text: A warehouse records the number of items inside each of $50$ parcels and also measures the mass, $m$ kilograms, of each parcel. The grouped frequency table summarises the masses of the $50$ parcels.

parts.label: (a)
parts.prompt: Explain why the mass of a parcel is continuous data, whereas the number of items inside the parcel is discrete data.
markscheme: Mass is measured and can take any value on a continuous scale (e.g. $2.35$ kg) [B1]
The number of items is counted and can only take whole-number values [B1]

parts.label: (b)
parts.prompt: The mass of one parcel is recorded as $4.6$ kg, correct to $1$ decimal place. Write down the lower bound and the upper bound of the actual mass of this parcel.
parts.answer_format: Lower bound = ..... kg , Upper bound = ..... kg

parts.label: (c)
parts.prompt: The number of items inside another parcel is $n$, where $12 < n \le 15$. Write down all the possible values of $n$.
markscheme: $13, 14, 15$ [B2] (or any two correct with no extras [B1])

parts.label: (d)
parts.prompt: Calculate an estimate of the mean mass of the $50$ parcels.

intro_text: The histogram shows information about the time, $t$ minutes, that a group of visitors spent in an art gallery.

parts.label: (a)
parts.prompt: Explain why the bars in this histogram are drawn touching each other with no gaps, whereas a bar chart for discrete data has gaps between the bars.
markscheme: Time is continuous data, so there are no gaps between adjacent class intervals [B1]
Discrete data takes separate distinct values, so gaps between bars show that intermediate values do not exist [B1]

parts.label: (b)
parts.prompt: Use the histogram to show that the total number of visitors in this group is $90$.
markscheme: Calculating frequencies from bar areas: $10 \times 1.5 = 15$ and $15 \times 2.4 = 36$ [M1]

parts.label: (c)
parts.prompt: In the gallery gift shop, a researcher also records the number of postcards bought by each of the $90$ visitors. State whether this data is discrete or continuous, and explain why it would not be valid to represent this data with a smooth continuous curve.
markscheme: The number of postcards can only take integer values ($0, 1, 2, \dots$) [B1]
Points on a smooth curve between integer values would have no meaning because fractional numbers of postcards cannot be bought [B1]

parts.label: (d)
parts.prompt: An additional $k$ visitors later enter the gallery, all spending between $10$ and $25$ minutes. When their times are included, the relative frequency of a visitor spending more than $25$ minutes becomes $\dfrac{3}{8}$. Find the value of $k$.
markscheme: Number of visitors spending more than $25$ minutes $= 27 + 12 = 39$ [B1]

intro_text: The daily temperatures, in degrees Celsius, recorded at a weather station over 12 days are shown below. \\[0.15cm] \begin{center} $7$ \quad $3$ \quad $5$ \quad $26$ \quad $4$ \quad $8$ \\[0.15cm] $5$ \quad $10$ \quad $2$ \quad $6$ \quad $9$ \quad $5$ \end{center}

parts.label: (a)
parts.prompt: Write down the mode.

parts.label: (b)
parts.prompt: Work out

subparts.label: (i)
subparts.prompt: the median,
markscheme: Ordered list: $2, 3, 4, 5, 5, 5, 6, 7, 8, 9, 10, 26$ or identifying middle values $5$ and $6$ [M1]

subparts.label: (ii)
subparts.prompt: the interquartile range.

parts.label: (c)
parts.prompt: The mean of these temperatures is $7.5$ degrees Celsius. Explain why the median is a more appropriate average than the mean to represent a typical daily temperature for this data.
markscheme: There is an extreme outlier of $26$ degrees Celsius [B1]
The median is not affected by extreme values, whereas the mean is pulled higher by $26$ [B1]

subparts.label: (i)
subparts.prompt: Show that $p + q = 21$.
markscheme: Sum of $x$-values for the $9$ plotted apartments $= 58$ and sum of $y$-values $= 121$ [B1]
Mean point $(\bar{x}, \bar{y}) = \left(\dfrac{58 + p}{10}, \dfrac{121 + q}{10}\right)$ lies on $y = -x + 20$, so $\dfrac{121 + q}{10} = -\dfrac{58 + p}{10} + 20$ [M1]

subparts.label: (ii)

parts.label: (d)
parts.prompt: Write down the coordinates of the mean point $(\bar{x}, \bar{y})$ for all $10$ apartments.
